standard: UK Cyber Security Council SPCC v4.2 with the Incident Response contextualisation (v2)

profile.name: Danny Howett
profile.conf: Client names, systems, threat actor details and some figures have been anonymised or omitted because of legal, contractual and security obligations. Each example accurately reflects my own responsibilities, the work I delegated, the authority I worked under, the decisions I made and the outcomes achieved. My referees can verify the substance of these claims.

evidence.title: Ransomware incident impacting a multinational telecommunications provider
evidence.scale: Large, interconnected network spanning multiple countries, with several thousand staff
evidence.situation: The client suffered a double extortion Ransomware attack encrypting servers in multiple countries and data theft, this impacted telephony services for some customers, as well as critical non customer facing systems.  The client was unknown to us previously, this was a matter which was referred to us for investigation by their cyber insurer, so we had no prior knowledge of their environment.  The incident involved various parties including the clients exec team, IT team, Legal and DPO as well as external cyber insurer and legal counsel.
evidence.task: The key immediate priority was to restore telephony services for affected end users, followed by the restoration of critical, then non business critical services.  In parallel, regulators needed to be kept updated (with varying levels of obligation across multiple countries), and I also led the workstream for threat actor engagement, used initially to help establish whether data had been exfiltrated and ascertain their demands.
evidence.action:
In the first hours, stakeholders on the call could not confirm whether the network was segmented. I recommended isolating the network to stop the spread without knowing whether every part of it could be affected. This carried significant business disruption, but I could not risk further encryption, which would have set recovery back by weeks and caused wider customer disruption. The decision proved correct.

I led an investigative DFIR team (this typically contained 5-10 team members throughout the lifecycle of the engagement), initially splitting it roughly 50/50 between containment and collecting the evidence needed for recovery, such as IOCs and persistent access, and defined an agreed reporting mechanism to provide regular updates to the client (but which also allowed the team space and time to investigate as well). All updates maintained legal privilege. Support was also provided with regulatory notifications, providing timely answers to provide updates to organisations such as the ICO.  I gave the insurer a projected run rate at the start and reported costs weekly for its approval.

The initial focus was on restoring key customer facing services and stopping any further spread.  This involved working with the clients IT and infrastructure teams to establish which hosts were impacting their availability services, and conduct a triage assessment whilst validating whether backups were viable, and using those that were once the triage assessment had validated a known clean state.  In parallel, containment efforts involved isolating affected parts of the network environment, preparing EDR tooling for deployment and triaging other high value hosts for "quick wins" in identification of IOCs to aid recovery efforts, and remove persistent access (C2, backdoors etc)

Once customer and business critical services were restored, the engagement moved into a wider phase, establishing root cause, validating data exfiltration claims and removing persistence. A new, isolated environment was stood up to aid recovery efforts, moving hosts declared as clean into a DMZ where EDR was deployed for monitoring and hunting at scale, and only when fully satisfied were hosts moved back into production.  The engagement lasted for approximately three months.
evidence.result: Customer facing services were restored within 48 hours (with the majority achieved within 24-36 hours) - the majority of critical services (allowing day to day business functions and those involving customer interactions (e.g. support or account management) were restored in under a week.  The total engagement lasted for around three months before the environment was fully validated and all systems restored.  This was aided by the successful provision of a decryption tool which sped recovery up, although this was at considerable expense, we negotiated a substantial reduction in the original demand. It was necessary in this case to engage with the threat actors for this purpose as some key business systems could not be recovered, and would have to be rebuilt at significant time and effort. All relevant sanctions and other checks were completed and passed in this regard, and the risks associated with this action were fully explained to the board.  On a later call, the client's infrastructure team established that the network was not fully segmented: had we not isolated it, other parts would have been encrypted and additional services affected.
evidence.followup: Following investigation of the incident, a post incident review was held with key IT and exec stakeholders where several areas were identified for improvement, along with a summary of what had worked well in the aftermath of the incident.  All recommendations were provided with named owners, this included ourselves, who despite having no prior connection to the organisation were retained for a significant programme of proactive and readiness services, in addition to a multi-year managed service covering a range of offensive and defensive support frameworks.  The run rate tracked closely to the projection, with the insurer approving costs weekly, and the client went on to spend a six-figure sum on proactive services.

evidence.title: Forensics support civil litigation matter
evidence.scale: Forensic Examination of 15+ devices capable of storing digital media
evidence.situation: The client, a manufacturing firm was seeking to take action against a former employee who had left the organisation in order to start a rival company up in Malaysia, using lower cost production tooling and workforce.  It was alleged that the employee had taken a large amount of the companies intellectual property with him.
evidence.task: My task was to perform forensic analysis on a range of devices capable of storing digital media.   This included laptops, mobile phones, external media as well as cloud storage and email belonging to the ex-employee (which I was permitted to analyse via a court order) - to establish whether there was any evidence to support the clients claims.
evidence.action: I performed forensic examination of the devices aligned to recognised best practices (ACPO Good practice guide for digital evidence, ISO/IEC 27037:2012) with the aim of keeping original evidence unaltered, recording all actions (in both note and visual form where appropriate) ensuring that an independent examiner could reproduce my findings.  All devices were in a powered off state when received, and after photographing each evidence item a physical image created, verifying each sources hash, maintaining chain of custody and evidence integrity throughout.  Forensic analysis was conducted on a dedicated, clean workstation using a range of commercial forensic tools for which I had both appropriate training and experience.
evidence.result: Examination of the devices supported the clients claims that intellectual property had been taken without authority.  Whilst the majority of devices appeared to be "clean" significant evidence was found within an iCloud backup on a Mac device.  A messaging app chat was recovered between the ex-employee and other persons during which compelling evidence was found to support the allegation, also several web searches relating to the sound destruction of data and removal of search history.  An additional chat application was identified after reviewing the primary messaging platform where evidence was found of widespread data theft, an app described by the ex-employee as "not on their radar"
evidence.followup: I provided an affidavit of my findings to support the clients case, and later gave expert witness testimony at Malaysian court.  The client achieved a successful outcome in their claim.

evidence.title: Runbook/Playbook testing and creation
evidence.scale: Creation of 6 x runbooks and IR plan
evidence.situation: We took on a range of managed services supporting our client, one of which was DFIR.  The client had previously outsourced this to a third-party.  During a knowledge transfer handover it was established that the previous IR plan was outdated, and there were no runbook scenarios, posing a risk
evidence.task: I was responsible for designing and delivering an IRP, and runbooks for the most likely and highest impact scenarios (validated through Intelligence linked to the clients sector / geography and other factors, and client discussions).
evidence.action: The Incident Response plan was aligned to the core Incident response lifecycle (NIST SP 800-61 r3), and ISO/IEC 27035, defining roles and responsibilities, severity classifications and communications channels and escalations. For each of the runbooks, I wrote step by step procedures covering detection, triage, containment, eradication, recovery and evidence preservation, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques.  All commands and queries e.g. KQL were tested and validated in the actual environment to ensure that they were 1) working, and 2) appropriate.
evidence.result: The organisation now has a formally agreed, up to date IRP and six validated runbooks, adopted as the standard for the SOC/IR teams.  An annual review cycle (or on any major vendor or network change) has been implemented to ensure they remain fit for use.
evidence.followup: The runbooks have since been used in real incidents. At the end of each incident a lessons learned session gathers feedback from senior stakeholders and those who played a large part in the response, and this feeds into an updated version of the runbooks.

evidence.title: Tabletop devise and deliver - global news outlet
evidence.scale: Global news outlet - C suite tabletop
evidence.situation: The client approached us after recently having a cyber incident involved a BYOD user device, where malware was able to get into the primary network environment.  Despite the attack being unsuccessful, the client had addressed the vulnerabilities that led to the attack, but wanted this, and decision making tested, as this was unclear had also slowed down their response capability.  The in person tabletop was attended by Exec team members from London, Germany and Hong Kong, as well as key IT stakeholders from across the business
evidence.task: I first held scoping sessions with the clients IT team, understanding bespoke and commercial tooling, and what had occurred during the near miss, this was used to ensure that the scenario was realistic and the ask was clearly defined. The scenario needed to test the organisations readiness in response to a successful, significant malware infection, which would test the incident response plan, identify gaps in decision making and co-ordination
evidence.action: I built a realistic scenario using the framework of the previous incident, but escalating the attack to a significant malware incident involving data exfiltration and extortion.  Current Threat actor tactics were researched and used.  The exercise used timed injected testing both strategic and technical decisions, the business impact and prioritisation, and moved into regulatory notification, ransom payment and sanctions considerations, as well as handling media and PR.  I facilitated the discussion, with the team capturing decisions in real time.  After the event feedback was sought, and we followed up with a post incident exercise report setting out our findings and recommendations.  A further call was held with IT to agree these and assign named owners to each with deadlines.  I challenged the client's playbook by asking what would happen if the named decision makers were not available. The playbook named people for critical business decisions but had no fallback, which led to a discussion about who could make near-instant business decisions in the heat of an incident.  I had three to four weeks to prepare, with two researchers supporting me while I designed the exercise. I built it around the client's own in-house and proprietary systems so non-technical attendees would recognise them, produced a briefing pack for delegates, and ran it in-house twice beforehand, fixing a couple of injects that worked on paper but not in practice.
evidence.result: The exercise was well received by the client, and identified several gaps
evidence.followup: A couple of weeks later I met the IT team who commissioned the exercise. They had gathered feedback from attendees and agreed a couple of practical improvements to implement immediately, with a roadmap for further changes, including regular real-world testing of procedures that had only been documented on paper, such as retrieving and reintroducing backups. I track progress through regular monthly calls with the client.

evidence.title: L&D Training Pathways
evidence.scale: Six career frameworks for the team, plus one-to-one mentoring
evidence.situation: In my current role I volunteered to support the Learning and Development (L&D) function for the team.
evidence.task: Develop a range of career pathways for the team, and mentor a junior team member who wants to transition from a Security Operations Centre (SOC) role into DFIR.
evidence.action: I developed six career frameworks aligned to SFIA 9 (the Skills Framework for the Information Age): SOC, DFIR, a SOC-to-DFIR transition pathway, Governance, Risk and Compliance (GRC), Offensive Security, and Security Advisory and Consulting. Each sets out grades mapped to SFIA levels of responsibility and skills, with recommended certifications, professional bodies (including CIISec, UKCSC, CREST and BCS), a gap analysis and curated learning resources. The SOC-to-DFIR pathway maps the skills a SOC analyst already has to their DFIR equivalents and highlights the gaps to close. Alongside this, I mentor a junior team member who wants to move from the SOC into DFIR.
evidence.result: The six frameworks are complete. My mentee is working through the SOC-to-DFIR pathway; their transition is still in progress.
evidence.followup: The pathway gives my mentee and me an agreed set of skills gaps to work through.

evidence.title: Delivery of Monthly Threat Intelligence Webinars
evidence.situation: Devise and deliver a monthly threat intelligence webinar
evidence.task: I curated and delivered a monthly threat intelligence webinar, available to all.  This was shared on LinkedIn by myself and my organisation.  I have done this in my past two roles, with a peak of >120 attendees from 15+ countries
evidence.action: I curate each session from current threat reporting and present it live; it is open to all, and both my organisation and I share it on LinkedIn.
evidence.result: Feedback was positive, and attendee logs show people regularly returning to later sessions. The webinar grew without advertising from zero to 125 attendees from 15+ countries at the most recent session.
evidence.followup: Based on attendee feedback, I moved from broad monthly sessions to quarterly sector-based webinars, covering sectors such as transport and logistics in depth.

evidence.title: Guest on the Richmond Advisory Group "Cyber Sidekicks" podcast
evidence.situation: I was invited as a guest on the Richmond Advisory Group "Cyber Sidekicks" podcast during Cyber Awareness Month (October 2025), as Technical Director at CyXcel.
evidence.task: Share practical insight from DFIR with a business audience.
evidence.action: I discussed what is happening in AI and in digital forensics and incident response (DFIR), and how businesses can build their cyber resilience.
evidence.result: The episode was published and remains publicly available.

evidence.title: Achieved ISO27001, NCSC CIR Standard and Cyber Essentials in first year as DFIR lead
evidence.situation: As DFIR lead, I saw the importance of gaining industry recognised accreditations.
evidence.task: Achieve ISO/IEC 27001, NCSC Cyber Incident Response (CIR) Standard and Cyber Essentials accreditation in my first year as DFIR lead, sponsored by the CEO.
evidence.action: We were starting from scratch, but I knew these accreditations were year-one objectives, so I built the forensic tooling and operating model around their requirements from the outset. I set audit and assessment dates with plenty of notice, used a dashboard to validate outstanding tasks before each assessment, held twice-weekly team calls dedicated to the audits, and regularly validated that we stayed aligned.
evidence.result: Passed all three first time, within my first year as DFIR lead.
evidence.followup: I keep an audit trail of everything each accreditation requires us to evidence and make sure it is recorded every month. For the NCSC CIR scheme I report monthly on the number and types of incidents we investigate. For ISO/IEC 27001, I check that any new technology or infrastructure meets its requirements before we bring it on board. The aim is not only to meet each objective but to be able to evidence it at audit.

evidence.title: Devise and Deliver Threat Intelligence Workstream
evidence.situation: As DFIR lead, threat intelligence is vital both to support investigations, and prevent them.  Without an intelligence capability, we were limited in our ability to attribute activity, anticipate attacker behaviour, and advise clients beyond the immediate incident.  There was also a missed commercial opportunity, clients increasingly want a broader service that covers both reactive and proactive services.  This was a service that I had done the same with in my previous role, which was delivering 15% of total IR revenue across reactive and retainers.
evidence.task: I was responsible for devising and delivering a threat intelligence product offering with two aims.  Firstly to strengthen our incident response capability with timely intelligence, and to establish a standalone service offering with a clear market differentiator
evidence.action: I designed the workstream around the Intelligence lifecycle, testing several commercial intelligence products that would complement the teams own dark web persona footprint, capability and open source tooling.  As well as monitoring for client exposure and risk, the offering mapped their critical supply chain (assessed through stakeholder interviews) and monitored high level exposure (such as Company X has had 50 malware stealer infections in the past month, or company Y suffered a Ransomware attack which your data may be in) - this approach helped the organisation to better understand and take action on risk.  New hires were trained on supporting threat intelligence from the outset, with clearly defined methodologies, template and tooling.  The product was taken to market in co-ordination with the marketing team and was well received by our clients.
evidence.result: Intelligence quickly formed part of the Incident Response process.  From the outset, the team was gathering intelligence (current TTPs, IOCs and campaigns) to support engagements, and improving the speed of our detection of malicious activity. Supply chain coverage was prominent in our success (aided by the product launch around the time of numerous high profile Ransomware incidents where threat actors were aided by supply chain compromise)

evidence.title: Opswat Academy Bootcamp
evidence.situation: Protecting CNI and OT is a fast moving and specialised area of security, where threats can quickly turn into a critical incident.  Formal training to support defence is important for capability and improving my own knowledge in this area.
evidence.task: Attend the Opswat academy Bootcamp and complete its certification to deepen my expertise in CNI protection, OT/ICS security and threat prevention, whilst generating valuable CPD to support my own ongoing certifications and professional memberships
evidence.action: I completed the two-day, in-person OPSWAT Academy Bootcamp.
evidence.result: I passed the certification for the OPSWAT MetaDefender platform and logged the CPD in my SANS account towards GCFA recertification.

evidence.title: Forensic IR tool
evidence.situation: The DFIR community relies on a range of commercial tools for forensic investigations.  There are also many wonderful Open Source resources (Zimmerman Tools, Autopsy, Chainsaw, Hayabusa) that commonly form part of an analysts toolset.  I wanted to create a GUI based triage tool that would be complementary to both, but with the added value of automating threat hunting against common financially motivated threat actor TTPs
evidence.task: In planning for the tool I researched tools that were commonly used, and which aspects would be most useful for my tool.  One area that was commonly overlooked was the automation of threat hunting against known TTPs / IOCs used by the most prolific Ransomware groups.  Other "must haves" included a visual timeline view for identifying spikes in activity, the ability to pivot around an event, and the ability to both tag and export artefacts
evidence.action: I created the tool from scratch, with development accelerated by Claude AI.  It has the ability to parse several host artefacts, including MFT, EVTX, Prefetch, Amcache/Shimcache, Browser History with all evidence items hashed, and an ingest log included to maintain integrity.  The tool threat hunts in the background, with the output presenting findings to the user assessed as high/critical/medium for further review.  Users can tag items, pivot around findings of interest, and view an activity graph to find spikes in logging to aid detections.  The tool has a search feature, and is able to ingest "IOC lists" for multiple queries, findings are exportable in multiple formats, including CSV, STIX and HTML.  All findings are mapped to MITRE ATT&CK
evidence.result: fx v0.1.4 is currently released on GitHub, and has been used in the wild on a range of projects by myself and other users.
evidence.followup: This is an active project under ongoing development and improvement.  Feedback and ideas are sought from users

evidence.title: IR/Readiness/Intelligence/OT tools
evidence.situation: DFIR and intelligence work often happens in isolated or air gapped environments, or on client sites with no approved tooling.  Commercial and open source tooling is often fragmented, behind paywalls or built as cloud services where sensitive data cannot be uploaded
evidence.task: Create a suite of free, open source tools covering the Incident Response lifecycle and readiness and assessment work that frames this.
evidence.action: I designed and built a suite of fully client side tools, written in HTML and with development accelerated by AI.  The set spans the full incident lifecycle (e.g. TRACE for case management, email header and PowerShell analysis, file hashing and a Textdiff tool for DFIR), ATT&CK mapping, threat actor references for Intelligence, and assessment frameworks (NCSC CAF, Cyber and Phishing programme maturity and OT Field/Reference guides).  All tools are mapped to recognised frameworks, and packaged as an open source, accessible collection on GitHub
evidence.result: A free, open source toolkit of 40+ tools to support the DFIR community that work anywhere with no data uploads, supporting responders across the whole incident lifecycle.

evidence.title: Technical commentary on the DDoS attack on X (Times Radio / Daily Mail coverage)
evidence.situation: On 10 March 2025, X (formerly Twitter) suffered a significant distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack that caused outages for users worldwide over several hours.
evidence.task: Support my organisation's media response: a colleague was interviewed by Times Radio and the Daily Mail, and I was asked to provide the detailed technical explanation.
evidence.action: I explained how the attack unfolded in multiple waves through the day, the group that claimed responsibility, and the steps organisations can take to protect themselves against DDoS attacks.
evidence.result: My organisation published my explanation on LinkedIn alongside the Times Radio interview and the Daily Mail article.

evidence.title: Recommendation for former colleague
evidence.situation: A former colleague reached out to me asking for a LinkedIn recommendation to support them in looking for a new role.
evidence.task: Provide a recommendation that would support their job search.
evidence.action: I wrote a LinkedIn recommendation for them.
evidence.result: The recommendation is published on their LinkedIn profile to support their search.

evidence.title: Article Contribution for the Daily Mail
evidence.situation: I was asked to contribute towards a Daily Mail article on the risks posed by SMS messages
evidence.task: I was requested by our marketing team to provide a short (750 word) article outlining common dangers associated with SMS / text messaging, with a tight delivery lead time for publication
evidence.action: I provided an article aligned to the brief.  This included risks around social engineering, spoofing and trust, and authentication weaknesses, as well as malware and device risks, alongside sensible mitigations
evidence.result: An excerpt from my article was included in the Daily Mail article in February 2025.

evidence.title: Community sharing of phishing domains following the CrowdStrike outage
evidence.situation: After the CrowdStrike outage in July 2024, caused by a faulty software update, new CrowdStrike-themed domains were being registered every day, many likely to be used for phishing and malware.
evidence.task: Collate newly registered phishing domains and share them with the community.
evidence.action: From 20 July 2024 I collated newly registered CrowdStrike domains in a shared Google Sheet, highlighting each day's new domains in red, and posted daily updates on X and LinkedIn, tagging other researchers tracking the same activity.
evidence.result: Individual updates reached around 160 to 180 views each, giving defenders a free, current list of suspicious domains to block or monitor.

evidence.title: Attend Conferences (BlackHat, BSides, InfoSec Europe etc)
evidence.situation: DFIR and intelligence moves quickly, as do the TTPs used by attackers, and the tooling that supports investigations (even more so with AI) - lots of knowledge surfaces at the conferences and communities around them
evidence.task: Keep my DFIR and CTI awareness current and engage with similar professionals by attending a mix of commercial and community conferences, Black Hat for technical research and emerging defensive and offensive capability, InfoSec Europe for the broader market and governance picture, and BSides for practitioner led events, meeting colleagues, improving relationships and using what I learn as self improvement
evidence.action: I regularly attend these events, and have attended BlackHat for the past three years, and InfoSec Europe, and have upcoming attendance at BlackHat and BSides London in December 2026.  I have also previously spoken at conferences, providing a talk for the Bedford branch of BCS whilst still in law enforcement, and given various lectures to colleagues in the Police on a range of subjects previously including (Darkweb, S49 RIPA, Cyber Crime and Digital currencies)
evidence.result: Attendance counts towards my 20 to 40 hours of formal CPD a year, which I record in my SANS account for GCFA recertification.

evidence.title: Professional Memberships - CIISec
evidence.situation: I am an Affiliate member of the Chartered Institute of Information Security (CIISec) through my employer.
evidence.task: Work to CIISec's code of conduct.
evidence.action: I apply its principles in my casework, for example obtaining written authorisation before accessing personal data.
evidence.result: See EV-027 for an example of the code shaping a decision.

evidence.title: High Volume Insurance Led IR work
evidence.scale: 500+ incident response engagements over the past five years in consultancy roles
evidence.situation: Over the past five years in consultancy roles I have worked on more than 500 incident response engagements, many of them insurance-led.
evidence.task: Lead investigations into ransomware, nation-state activity, business email compromise (BEC), network intrusion and other incident types, while managing clients, budgets and the investigating team.
evidence.action: I led investigations across these incident types, managing the client relationship, the engagement budget and the team on each engagement.
evidence.result: Across this period my firm sat on six to ten insurer panels for large global organisations across EMEA, primarily the UK and with significant work in South Africa.

evidence.title: Examining locked devices under legal authority (policing)
evidence.situation: In my policing role I routinely examined devices that were locked or whose passcodes were not available.
evidence.task: Recover evidence from these devices lawfully, within the legal framework and with the required authority.
evidence.action: I used specialist tools such as GrayKey and Cellebrite, completed a course in Android debugging, and used password-cracking tools in Kali Linux, alongside examining other seized devices to help establish passwords. All of this was done within the legal framework and with the required authority.
evidence.result: Every examination was carried out within the legal framework and with the required authority.

evidence.title: Technical director: DFIR budget ownership
evidence.situation: As technical director I was responsible for the DFIR function's spend.
evidence.task: Set budgets across tooling, team and lab spend.
evidence.action: I produced a detailed budget assessment covering tooling, team and lab spend, aligned to estimated revenue.
evidence.result: The budget was approved after review. Lab spend came in slightly under budget because I repurposed existing equipment, and the lab was delivered on time with fully working, secure infrastructure that met all requirements.

evidence.title: Lunch-and-learn sessions (memory forensics, IR, threat intelligence, evidence integrity)
evidence.situation: Developing the team's DFIR skills alongside live casework, and closing gaps I saw in practice, such as incomplete chain of custody forms.
evidence.task: Share specialist knowledge with colleagues and make sure the team understands its legal and evidential obligations.
evidence.action: I have run four or five lunch-and-learn sessions: memory forensics with Volatility; incident response; threat intelligence, covering OSINT best practice and staying safe, particularly on dark web sites; and evidence integrity, covering chain of custody, how it is documented and recorded in systems, what to record on evidence bags, photographing evidence items (particularly damaged ones) and, where possible, recording devices being taken apart, so the full handling timeline can be reproduced and stands up to legal scrutiny.
evidence.result: Typically five to 15 team members attended, with senior management joining on occasions. Feedback was generally good.
evidence.followup: After each session I shared the slides and invited follow-up questions.

evidence.title: Impartial, evidence-based reporting and expert evidence
evidence.situation: As an expert witness and as the author of incident reports, my findings may be relied on by courts, regulators, insurers and boards. In DFIR it is common not to be able to fully establish root cause, for example because of limited log retention, log clearing or anti-forensics, and clients often see this as a failing.
evidence.task: Keep every finding impartial and evidence-based, whatever the client hopes to hear.
evidence.action: As an expert witness I understood that my role was impartial and based solely on factual evidence, or on my expert assessment where there were gaps. I only include findings in a report that I can corroborate with evidence. When root cause cannot be established, I explain the reasons fully rather than speculating. If I am pressed to overstate a finding, I push back and explain that, as the report's author, I could be liable for anything knowingly untrue.
evidence.result: In one engagement this meant reporting data exfiltration the client had hoped to rule out; the report went out as written and the client notified the ICO (see EV-026).

evidence.title: Calm, honest communication with a stressed client during ransomware recovery
evidence.situation: A manufacturer's encrypted systems had halted most of its operational capability, with losses of more than £1 million a day, and its leadership was under intense pressure.
evidence.task: Lead the response and give the client's leadership what they needed to make decisions under pressure.
evidence.action: I spoke clearly and calmly to explain the recovery process, how long it was likely to take, and how quickly we could restore the critical systems behind manufacturing. To restart critical systems quickly the client had to accept some risk, which I explained fully: the systems appeared clean but were not yet validated as free of malware or persistent access, and ideally we would keep them in an isolated environment until we were sure.
evidence.result: Critical manufacturing processes were back up within 48 hours. The client understood and accepted the risk, and later work confirmed the hosts had been cleaned, so production could return.

evidence.title: Fair, consistent hiring: graduate scheme and structured interviews
evidence.situation: In my previous role we needed to grow the team and bring new people into the profession fairly.
evidence.task: Recruit on the value candidates could bring, never on gender, race, ethnicity or any other protected characteristic.
evidence.action: We ran a graduate scheme that brought in final-year university students through a structured training pathway and a ten-week placement, with a view to full-time roles on graduation. In interviews we used the same question set for every candidate so competencies were assessed consistently. I also took part in my employer's community volunteering days, supporting projects such as homelessness charities.
evidence.result: The graduate scheme brought several junior team members into the profession.

evidence.title: Reporting data exfiltration the client had ruled out
evidence.situation: A client's internal investigation had found no evidence of data exfiltration. My investigation found evidence in the logs that personal and sensitive data had been exfiltrated, meaning notifications to the ICO and data subjects, and possible fines.
evidence.task: Report the findings accurately as investigation lead and report author.
evidence.action: I was asked to play the finding down in the report. I declined: the evidence in the logs was unambiguous, the report had to reflect it, and the client had a legal obligation to notify.
evidence.result: The report went out as written. The client notified the ICO; my team supported the notification and used e-discovery tools to assess the data and identify affected data subjects.

evidence.title: Written authorisation before accessing a cloud mailbox
evidence.situation: In the civil litigation matter, the client gave me a username, password and verbal permission to access a former employee's Gmail account.
evidence.task: Access the evidence only with proper authority.
evidence.action: I judged that verbal permission was not enough. Before accessing the account I asked for written authorisation from the client and from the account owner, and confirmed the legal framework that allowed the access.
evidence.result: I accessed the mailbox only once written authorisation and the legal basis were confirmed, so the evidence could be relied on in court.

evidence.title: Developing a multinational DFIR team (previous role)
evidence.situation: My previous role's DFIR practice had 15 to 20 people in the UK, 20 to 30 in the US and five to ten in India, with people managers at each grade running monthly and annual performance reviews.
evidence.task: Make sure the people I led were on track, had the skills they needed and could progress, within the training budget.
evidence.action: I held check-ins at least quarterly to confirm people were on track and their training needs were met, and to ask informally whether they were happy and what more we could do. We used a structured training pathway with a learning platform, and I identified paid training such as SANS and Firebrand courses according to what each person needed to reach the next grade, balanced against cost.
evidence.result: On several occasions staff were promoted to the next grade with additional responsibilities.

evidence.title: Forensic methodology documents (Windows, Linux, Mac, cloud)
evidence.situation: Analysts need a structured, repeatable way to investigate across operating systems and cloud platforms.
evidence.task: Maintain methodology aligned to recognised frameworks.
evidence.action: Our methodology documents cover Windows, Linux and Mac forensics and AWS, GCP and Azure, aligned to NIST and SANS incident response frameworks and the ACPO principles. I continually assess and update them for changes in attacker TTPs, including the growing use of AI to support attacks, so analysts can identify AI-driven activity.
evidence.result: Analysts have a repeatable approach that is kept current with attacker methods.

evidence.title: Tracking legal and regulatory change
evidence.situation: Much of my current work is with critical national infrastructure (CNI) organisations facing new regulation.
evidence.task: Keep my legal and regulatory knowledge current without trying to monitor everything.
evidence.action: I follow a structured process built on authoritative sources: NCSC alerts and bulletins, ICO updates, professional events and communities, and upcoming legislation such as the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill.
evidence.result: This shapes the UK forensic laboratory I am building, so that clients are compliant with new requirements from the outset.

evidence.title: Resolving executive and IT conflict over ransomware recovery timescales
evidence.situation: A medium-sized SME suffered a ransomware attack on a Friday evening. Its executives wanted to be fully up and running by Monday morning; its IT team pushed back that this could not be done in that time. Conflict like this between executives and IT is common during incidents.
evidence.task: Lead the response and agree a recovery pathway that both the executives and IT could support.
evidence.action: I explained that a full recovery by Monday was very rarely possible for an organisation of that size, and walked each group through the recovery steps. I used my firm's ransomware timeline, a document that takes organisations that have never suffered an attack through the typical process from attack to return to normal. Together we agreed to prioritise business-critical systems: those that were customer-facing and those essential to running the business.
evidence.result: The executives accepted residual risk: systems could come back online in a new environment before we could be 100% sure they were clean. The IT team stood up that new environment, and the rest of remediation followed agreed, tested processes, so business as usual could continue to a degree.
evidence.followup: I now use the ransomware timeline early with clients new to ransomware, to set realistic expectations before conflict builds.

evidence.title: Two-way peer review of client reports
evidence.situation: Every report my team produces goes to a client and may be relied on by insurers, regulators or courts.
evidence.task: Make sure every report is of the highest possible quality and accuracy before delivery.
evidence.action: Every report is peer reviewed before it reaches the client. I review my team's reports, and I always ask a team member to review mine objectively and identify anything that could be improved. In one review we found that a team member had reused a recent report rather than starting from the clean master template, and it still contained another client's information. I walked through with them why it had happened: the circumstances were similar to a recent job. I reminded them that our policy requires every incident to start from a new set of templates, with defined points in the incident lifecycle where a new template should be used.
evidence.result: The error was caught before the report went out, preventing a disclosure of another client's confidential information. The team member agreed they should not have done it, and I dealt with it through informal advice.
evidence.followup: The incident reinforced, across the team, the policy of starting each incident from clean master templates.

evidence.title: Adapting an investigation plan after discovering an undisclosed development environment
evidence.situation: On insurance-led work I often have no prior relationship with the client, and scoping calls can miss key information because the right people are busy or the questions do not surface it. During one investigation, my technical analysis found lateral movement from a development environment that had not been mentioned on any call and was outside our scope.
evidence.task: Follow the incident lifecycle (aligned to NIST, or SANS where it suits the client better) while adapting the plan as new information emerged, and keep the client and insurer informed.
evidence.action: I add a separate technical call with IT after scoping to catch what scoping misses. When the dev environment surfaced, I spoke to the client's technical team, who confirmed it was connected to production. Because the scope changed, I was transparent straight away about the change in cost, time and effort, explained why the extra work was needed to establish root cause, and sought approval from the client or their insurer before going ahead.
evidence.result: With approval, my team assessed the development environment and found that the threat actor had got in through it, establishing root cause.
evidence.followup: I treat scoping as continuous refinement and raise scope changes as early as possible.

evidence.title: Challenging poor evidence handling: incomplete chain of custody
evidence.situation: I regularly saw chain of custody forms that had been left incomplete, meaning I had to go back to individuals afterwards to validate information, which makes evidence harder to verify.
evidence.task: Challenge the practice and stop it recurring, so evidence stands up to legal scrutiny.
evidence.action: I went back to the individuals to validate the missing information, then ran a dedicated lunch-and-learn on evidence integrity: chain of custody and how it is documented and recorded in systems, what to record on evidence bags, photographing evidence items, especially damaged ones, and recording devices being taken apart where possible.
evidence.result: The team was given a clear, shared standard for evidence handling, so the full timeline of what happened to each item can be reproduced.
evidence.followup: Slides were shared afterwards, with an open invitation to follow up with questions.

evidence.title: Quality-assuring team CPD and training records
evidence.situation: In a previous role, training needed to be planned and its value checked across the team.
evidence.task: Make sure team members' learning was recorded, reviewed and fed into future training plans, and have my own reviewed in the same way.
evidence.action: Senior leaders, including me, ran a monthly training call that opened with forward-looking training requirements. In one-to-ones and appraisals I went through each person's learning, discussing not only what they had done but how they found it and whether it had proved valuable since.
evidence.result: That feedback shaped future training requirements for other staff. My own CPD was reviewed in the same way by those above me.

A1.situation: A multinational telecommunications provider suffered a double-extortion ransomware attack that encrypted servers in several countries, stole data and disrupted telephony for some customers. Its cyber insurer referred the incident to my firm, so I started with no knowledge of the environment, working with the client's executives, IT and legal teams, data protection officer (DPO), insurer and external counsel.
A1.task: I led the digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) engagement from start to finish and was accountable for the investigating team, reporting to the client, and cost reporting to the insurer. The priorities were restoring telephony, then critical and other services, while supporting regulatory updates in several countries.
A1.action: In the first hours, the stakeholders on the call could not confirm whether the network was segmented. I recommended isolating the network to stop the spread without knowing whether every part of it could be affected. Isolation meant significant business disruption, but further encryption would have set recovery back by weeks and widened customer impact, so I judged it the lower risk. I then led a team of five to ten, initially split between containment and collecting the evidence needed for recovery: indicators of compromise (IOCs) and the attacker's persistent access, such as command-and-control (C2) channels and backdoors. I restored services only from backups that triage showed were clean. Once critical services were back, I moved the team on to root cause, validating the attacker's data theft claims and removing persistence, and recovered hosts through an isolated network zone monitored with endpoint detection and response (EDR) tooling before returning them to production.
A1.result: On a later call, the client's infrastructure team established that the network was not fully segmented, so without isolation other parts would have been encrypted and more services affected. The team restored customer-facing services within 48 hours and most critical services within a week, and after around three months confirmed that all systems were restored.
A1.followup: I held a post-incident review that gave each improvement a named owner. Although the client had no prior relationship with my firm, it retained us for a significant readiness programme and a multi-year managed service.

A2.situation: A manufacturing firm planned legal action against a former employee who had left to set up a rival company in Malaysia using lower-cost production tooling and labour. The firm alleged that he had taken a large amount of its intellectual property. Any findings would have to stand up in court.
A2.task: I was responsible for the forensic examination of more than 15 devices and accounts belonging to the former employee, including laptops, mobile phones, external media, cloud storage and email, to establish whether any evidence supported the firm's claims. A court order set out what I was authorised to analyse. I drew on my experience in policing, where I routinely examined devices, including locked ones, under the required legal authority.
A2.action: I followed recognised good practice, the Association of Chief Police Officers (ACPO) Good Practice Guide for Digital Evidence and ISO/IEC 27037:2012, so that the original evidence stayed unaltered and an independent examiner could reproduce my findings. I recorded every action in notes and, where appropriate, photographs. All devices arrived powered off; I photographed each one, created a physical forensic image, verified each source's hash and maintained chain of custody throughout. I analysed the images on a dedicated, clean workstation using commercial forensic tools in which I am trained and experienced. Most devices appeared clean, but in an iCloud backup on a Mac I recovered a messaging app chat between the former employee and others that contained compelling evidence supporting the allegation, along with web searches about destroying data and removing search history. Reviewing that chat led me to a second messaging application, which the former employee described as "not on their radar", where I found evidence of widespread data theft.
A2.result: My examination found evidence supporting the firm's claim that its intellectual property had been taken without authority. I documented my findings in an affidavit to support the firm's case.
A2.followup: I later gave expert witness testimony in the Malaysian court, and the firm achieved a successful outcome in its claim.

A3.situation: My firm took on a range of managed services for a client, including digital forensics and incident response (DFIR). The client had previously outsourced incident response to a third party. During the knowledge-transfer handover I established that its incident response plan (IRP) was out of date and that it had no runbooks for specific scenarios, leaving it exposed if a major incident occurred.
A3.task: I was responsible for designing and delivering a new IRP and runbooks for the client's most likely and highest-impact scenarios. I selected six scenarios using threat intelligence relevant to the client's sector and geography, and confirmed them in discussions with the client, which owned formal approval of the plan.
A3.action: I aligned the IRP to the incident response lifecycle in the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) SP 800-61 Revision 3 and to ISO/IEC 27035, defining roles and responsibilities, severity classifications, communication channels and escalation routes. For each runbook I wrote step-by-step procedures covering detection, triage, containment, eradication, recovery and evidence preservation, and mapped them to MITRE ATT&CK techniques. I tested every command and query in the client's live environment, for example queries in Kusto Query Language (KQL), to confirm that each one worked and was appropriate for that environment.
A3.result: The client formally approved the new IRP and all six runbooks and adopted them as the standard for its security operations centre (SOC) and incident response teams.
A3.followup: I set up an annual review cycle, with an additional review after any major vendor or network change. The client has since used the runbooks in real incidents. After each one I hold a lessons-learned session with senior stakeholders and the people most involved in the response, and their feedback goes into an updated version of the runbooks.

B1.situation: A global news organisation had recently suffered a cyber incident in which malware on a personal device used for work (bring your own device, BYOD) reached its main network. The attack was unsuccessful and the client had fixed the vulnerabilities, but unclear decision-making had slowed its response, and it wanted that decision-making tested. Executives from London, Germany and Hong Kong attended in person, along with key IT stakeholders from across the business.
B1.task: I was responsible for designing and facilitating a tabletop exercise to test the organisation's readiness for a successful, significant malware infection, exercise its incident response plan, and identify gaps in decision-making and coordination. The client owned the resulting decisions and actions.
B1.action: I started by listening. I held scoping sessions with the client's IT team to understand their bespoke and commercial tooling and what had happened during the near miss, so the scenario would be realistic and its objectives clearly defined. I built the scenario on the real incident, escalating it to a significant malware attack with data exfiltration and extortion, using current threat actor tactics. Timed injects tested strategic and technical decisions, business impact and prioritisation, then moved into regulatory notification, ransom payment and sanctions considerations, and media handling. I facilitated the discussion between the executives and IT stakeholders while my team captured decisions in real time. I challenged one assumption directly by asking what would happen if the named decision-makers were not available. The client's playbook named individuals for critical business decisions but had no fallback, and my question opened a discussion about who could make near-instant business decisions in the heat of an incident.
B1.result: Client feedback after the event was positive, and the exercise identified several gaps. I wrote a post-exercise report setting out the findings and recommendations.
B1.followup: On a follow-up call with the IT team I agreed the recommendations and gave each an owner and deadline. Because this is an ongoing client relationship, I track progress in regular meetings, which confirm that the client has since started real-world testing of procedures that had only existed on paper, such as retrieving and restoring backups.

B2.situation: During a multinational ransomware response, some of the client's key business systems could not be recovered from backups and would otherwise have had to be rebuilt at significant cost and time. The client's board had to decide whether to engage with the threat actor, a decision carrying legal, sanctions, financial and reputational risk.
B2.task: I led the workstream for engaging with the threat actor and was responsible for advising the board on it. The decision itself sat with the board, advised by its legal counsel and cyber insurer.
B2.action: I first used the engagement to establish whether data had really been exfiltrated and what the threat actor was demanding, so the board's decision rested on evidence rather than the attacker's claims. I then set out the risks in plain terms. A decryptor might not be provided at all; even if one was, experience showed it was unlikely to be fully reliable, particularly on large datasets; re-infection and further extortion remained possible; and any promise to delete stolen data could only be taken at face value. I based this on my firm's experience of this threat actor and on advice from trusted cryptocurrency partners. I explained the sanctions checks required and had my team carry them out on the client's behalf. In parallel I advised on regulatory updates across several countries, supporting the client's updates to regulators such as the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO).
B2.result: The sanctions checks passed, confirming that engagement could go ahead. My workstream secured a substantial reduction in the original demand, and the decryption tool significantly sped up recovery of systems the team could not otherwise have restored quickly.
B2.followup: Once the board understood the risks, it questioned its options more closely. In my experience the decision to engage usually comes down to need, such as the absence of usable backups or data too sensitive to risk exposure, so I make sure boards understand the risks clearly before they reach that point.

B3.situation: Across more than 500 incident response engagements I have worked with IT teams, chief information security officers and staff under intense pressure. In one ransomware attack on a manufacturer, encrypted systems had halted most of the client's operational capability, with losses of more than £1 million a day, and its leadership needed to decide which parts of the business to restart first.
B3.task: I led the response and was responsible for supporting the client's people through it; decisions on which operations to restart, and what risk to accept, sat with the client. In my previous role I also took part in recruitment, where I was responsible for assessing candidates fairly.
B3.action: I spoke calmly and clearly, explaining the recovery process, how long it was likely to take, and how quickly the team could restore the critical systems behind manufacturing, so the leadership could make strategic decisions about what to restart first. To bring critical systems back quickly, the client had to accept some risk, and I explained it honestly: the systems appeared clean but were not yet confirmed free of malware or persistent access, and ideally they would stay isolated until that was confirmed. In recruitment I assess candidates on the value they can bring, never on gender, race, ethnicity or any other protected characteristic. Our recruitment used structured interviews with the same question set for every candidate, so competencies were assessed consistently, and a graduate scheme that brought final-year university students in through a structured training pathway and a ten-week placement, leading to full-time roles. I also took part in my employer's community volunteering, supporting projects such as homelessness charities.
B3.result: Critical manufacturing processes were back up within 48 hours. The client understood and accepted the residual risk, and later checks confirmed the hosts had been cleaned, so production could return. The graduate scheme brought several junior team members into the profession.
B3.followup: I take the same approach on every engagement: keeping clients calm and informed, and being open about the risks of each recovery option so they can make their own decisions.

B4.situation: Threat intelligence and cyber risk need explaining to very different audiences, from security practitioners to members of the public with no technical background.
B4.task: I am responsible for curating and presenting a regular threat intelligence webinar, open to anyone, which I have run in my last two roles. Separately, my organisation's marketing team asked me to write a 750-word article for the Daily Mail on the dangers of Short Message Service (SMS) text messaging, to a tight publication deadline.
B4.action: For the webinar, I select current threats and explain what they mean in practice for an audience that includes both practitioners and non-specialists. For the article, I wrote for a general readership, explaining social engineering, spoofing and misplaced trust in text messages, weaknesses in text-based authentication, and malware and device risks, with sensible steps readers could take to protect themselves. When a colleague was interviewed by Times Radio about the distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack on X (formerly Twitter) in March 2025, I provided the published technical explanation of how the attack unfolded and how organisations can protect themselves. In incident response I adapt in the same way: I usually provide reports in two formats, an executive version focused on what matters to senior leaders, namely cost, downtime, impact and reputation, with a brief summary of what happened and why, and a detailed technical report for IT teams with full findings and recommendations.
B4.result: Feedback on the webinar has been positive, and attendance logs show people regularly returning. It grew without advertising from zero to 125 attendees from more than 15 countries at the most recent session. The Daily Mail published an excerpt of my article in February 2025.
B4.followup: In response to attendee feedback, I moved from broad monthly webinars to quarterly sector-based sessions, covering sectors such as transport and logistics in depth.

C1.situation: Over the past five years in consultancy roles I have worked on more than 500 incident response engagements, many referred by cyber insurers, covering ransomware, nation-state activity, business email compromise (BEC) and network intrusion. My firm sat on six to ten insurer panels across Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA), mainly in the UK and South Africa. Insurers fund these engagements and expect clear cost forecasts and regular reporting.
C1.task: On the engagements I led, I was responsible for the investigating team, the client relationship and cost reporting; the insurer approved costs. As technical director I was also responsible for setting the digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) budget across tooling, team and laboratory spend.
C1.action: I produced a detailed budget assessment for tooling, team and laboratory spend, aligned to estimated revenue. On the largest engagement, a multinational ransomware response lasting around three months, I gave the insurer a projected run rate at the start and reported costs weekly for approval. I led up to ten people at a time, initially splitting the team roughly equally between containment and collecting evidence for recovery, then shifting effort to root cause and validated recovery. The first week meant very long hours, so I checked in regularly with each person to ask how they were and what support they needed. As the pace eased, I rotated staff in and out of the engagement, using capacity around training and holidays, to give people a break from the investigation.
C1.result: Costs tracked closely to the projected run rate, and the insurer approved them every week. The team restored customer-facing services within 48 hours and most critical services within a week.
C1.followup: The client was very happy with the outcome and went on to spend a six-figure sum on proactive services as part of an ongoing relationship.

C2.situation: In my previous role the digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) practice had 15 to 20 people in the UK, 20 to 30 in the United States and five to ten in India. People managers at each grade supported the staff in the grade below and ran monthly and annual performance reviews.
C2.task: I was responsible for developing the people I led: making sure they were on track, had the knowledge and skills for their work, and had a route to progress, while keeping training costs within budget.
C2.action: I held check-ins at least quarterly to confirm that people were on track, that their training needs were being met and that they had the skills their work required, and to ask informally whether they were happy and what more we could do to support them. We used a structured training pathway with a learning platform covering a wide range of topics, and I identified paid specialist training, such as SANS and Firebrand courses, according to what each person needed to reach the next grade, balanced against cost. I also led lunch-and-learn sessions for the team on topics including memory forensics and DFIR.
C2.result: On several occasions staff were promoted to the next grade with additional responsibilities, confirmed through the formal performance review process.
C2.followup: I apply the same approach in my current role. I train new hires to support threat intelligence from their first day, with defined methodologies, templates and tooling, and I have developed six career frameworks aligned to the Skills Framework for the Information Age (SFIA 9) to give the team clear routes for progression. I also mentor a junior colleague moving from the security operations centre (SOC) into DFIR.

C3.situation: A global news organisation, an existing client, asked me to run an in-person executive tabletop exercise after a near miss, with participants from London, Germany and Hong Kong. Many attendees were not technical, so the exercise had to feel familiar and realistic, run to time on the day, and produce outcomes the client could act on.
C3.task: I was responsible for planning and delivering the exercise end to end within three to four weeks. I designed the exercise myself and led two researchers who supported the preparation.
C3.action: I started with a call to agree the client's objectives, the attendees and what they wanted from the day. I built the scenario around the client's own in-house and proprietary systems, so non-technical attendees would recognise the applications, what they did and the data they held, and produced a briefing pack explaining the systems and each attendee's role. My researchers supported the scenario with research into current threat actor tactics. We ran the exercise in-house twice beforehand, which exposed a couple of injects that worked on paper but not in practice, and I fixed them before the day. On the day I kept the timed injects on schedule while my team captured decisions in real time. Afterwards I produced a comprehensive report with the lessons learned and a full walkthrough of the discussion.
C3.result: The exercise ran to schedule and identified several gaps. A couple of weeks later I met the IT team who had commissioned it; they had gathered feedback from attendees and agreed a couple of practical improvements to implement immediately, with a roadmap for further changes.
C3.followup: I track progress against that roadmap through my regular monthly calls with the client.

C4.situation: As digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) lead I am responsible for highly sensitive client evidence, including material under legal privilege. The team was starting from scratch, and our chief executive set ISO/IEC 27001, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) Cyber Incident Response (CIR) scheme at Standard level, and Cyber Essentials as objectives for my first year.
C4.task: I was responsible for achieving all three accreditations, sponsored by the chief executive, and for making sure the team worked to them day to day.
C4.action: Because I knew the accreditations were year-one objectives, I built our forensic tooling and operating model around their requirements from the outset rather than retrofitting controls later. I set audit and assessment dates with plenty of notice, used a dashboard to validate any outstanding tasks before each assessment, and held twice-weekly team calls dedicated to the audits. Between assessments I regularly checked that our practice stayed aligned to the standards. I apply the same discipline in casework: in a civil litigation matter I examined more than 15 devices on a dedicated, clean workstation, verified the hash of every source, maintained chain of custody, and recorded every action so an independent examiner could reproduce my findings. On incident response engagements I keep all updates to clients under legal privilege.
C4.result: The team passed all three audits and assessments first time, within my first year as DFIR lead.
C4.followup: I keep an audit trail of everything each accreditation requires us to evidence and make sure it is recorded every month. For the NCSC CIR scheme I report monthly on the number and types of incidents we investigate. For ISO/IEC 27001, I check that any new technology or infrastructure meets its requirements before we bring it on board. The aim is not only to meet each objective but to be able to evidence it at audit.

D1.situation: I spent 13 years in policing, where honesty and integrity underpin every investigation, and I bring the same standard to incident response. In one engagement the client's own internal investigation had found no evidence of data exfiltration. My investigation then found evidence in the logs that personal and sensitive data had been exfiltrated, which meant notifications to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and to affected individuals, and possible fines.
D1.task: As investigation lead and report author, I was responsible for reporting the findings accurately. The decision to notify sat with the client, which had a legal obligation to do so if the evidence showed a reportable breach.
D1.action: I was asked to play the finding down in the report, and I declined. My reports are based on facts and evidence, with expert assessment only where there are gaps and clearly labelled as such. Here the evidence was not ambiguous: the logs showed a certain volume of data had left the network. I explained that the report had to reflect the evidence and that the client had a legal obligation to notify. Whenever I am pressed to change a finding, I also explain that, as the report's author, I could be liable for anything I knowingly state that is not true.
D1.result: The client accepted the report as written and notified the ICO, and my team supported the notification and used e-discovery tools to assess the exfiltrated data and identify the affected data subjects.
D1.followup: I apply the same principle when I cannot establish root cause, for example because of limited log retention, log clearing or anti-forensics. Clients can see this as a failing, so I explain the reasons fully rather than speculating to give them an answer.

D2.situation: Forensic investigation often involves access to personal data, such as email accounts and cloud storage, where acting without proper authority could breach the law and harm the people involved. In a civil litigation matter, the client gave me a username and password and verbal permission to examine a former employee's Gmail account.
D2.task: I am bound by the codes and principles I work to: the code of conduct of the Chartered Institute of Information Security (CIISec), through my membership; the Association of Chief Police Officers (ACPO) principles for digital evidence; and, as an expert witness, my duty to the court. I am responsible for applying them in my own work and in the investigations I lead.
D2.action: I judged that verbal permission was not enough. Before accessing the account I asked for written authorisation from both the client and the account owner, and confirmed the legal framework that allowed the access. The same principles guide all my work: acting in the public and organisational interest; reporting findings accurately and objectively, clearly separating fact from assumption; protecting confidentiality, including where and how we hold and encrypt data; accessing only the data an investigation needs, to protect the privacy of employees, customers and third parties; never exceeding authorised access or using it for any other purpose; working within my competence and bringing in specialists where needed; avoiding conflicts of interest; and keeping an audit trail of what I did and why.
D2.result: I accessed the mailbox only once written authorisation and the legal basis were confirmed, so the evidence could be relied on in court. I later gave expert evidence in the Malaysian court, and the client achieved a successful outcome.
D2.followup: My audit trail of each investigation also feeds into lessons learned afterwards.

D3.situation: Incident response often involves legal and regulatory obligations under time pressure. In a multinational ransomware response, the client had notification obligations to regulators in several countries, each with different requirements, and any engagement with the threat actor carried sanctions risk. In a separate civil litigation matter, my forensic work had to be lawful and admissible in a Malaysian court.
D3.task: I was responsible for making sure my own and my team's work complied with these requirements, and for supporting clients in meeting theirs. Decisions on notification and payment sat with the clients and their legal advisers.
D3.action: In the ransomware response I kept all updates to the client under legal privilege, supported its regulatory notifications with timely answers for updates to regulators such as the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), and made sure all sanctions and other checks were completed before engagement with the threat actor went ahead. In the litigation matter I analysed the former employee's cloud storage and email only under the authority of a court order, followed the Association of Chief Police Officers (ACPO) Good Practice Guide for Digital Evidence and ISO/IEC 27037:2012, and maintained chain of custody throughout. Earlier, in policing, I routinely examined locked devices using specialist tools such as GrayKey and Cellebrite, always within the legal framework and with the required authority.
D3.result: The sanctions checks confirmed that engagement could go ahead lawfully. In the litigation matter I provided an affidavit and gave expert witness testimony in the Malaysian court, and the client achieved a successful outcome.
D3.followup: Rather than trying to monitor everything, I follow a structured process built on authoritative sources: National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) and ICO alerts and bulletins, professional events and communities, and upcoming legislation such as the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill. Much of my current work is with critical national infrastructure (CNI) organisations, and this shapes the UK forensic laboratory I am building, so clients are compliant with new requirements from the outset.

D4.situation: Clients, insurers and courts expect incident response to follow recognised standards. As digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) lead I decide which standards apply to my team's work and to the plans I deliver for clients.
D4.task: I am responsible for identifying the standards relevant to my team's services and implementing them, both in our own accreditations and in work for clients.
D4.action: In my first year as DFIR lead I achieved ISO/IEC 27001, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) Cyber Incident Response (CIR) scheme at Standard level, and Cyber Essentials for the team. I built our forensic tooling and operating model around their requirements from the outset. When a managed service client's incident response plan (IRP) was out of date, I aligned the replacement to the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) SP 800-61 Revision 3 incident response lifecycle and to ISO/IEC 27035, and mapped six runbooks to MITRE ATT&CK techniques. In forensic examinations I follow the Association of Chief Police Officers (ACPO) Good Practice Guide for Digital Evidence and ISO/IEC 27037:2012.
D4.result: The team passed all three accreditation assessments first time. The client formally approved the new IRP and adopted it as the standard for its security operations centre (SOC) and incident response teams.
D4.followup: The client's IRP has an annual review cycle, with additional reviews after any major vendor or network change. I also keep our methodology documents current: repeatable approaches for Windows, Linux and Mac forensics and for Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud Platform (GCP) and Microsoft Azure, aligned to NIST and SANS frameworks. I update them for changes in attacker tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs), including the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in attacks.

E1.situation: Digital forensics, incident response and threat intelligence change quickly: attacker tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) and investigative tooling evolve constantly, even more so with artificial intelligence (AI). Protecting critical national infrastructure (CNI) and operational technology (OT) is a fast-moving, specialised area where threats can quickly become critical incidents.
E1.task: I am responsible for keeping my digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) and cyber threat intelligence (CTI) knowledge current and for recording my continuing professional development (CPD) to support my certifications and professional memberships.
E1.action: I attend a deliberate mix of conferences: Black Hat, which I have attended for the past three years, for technical research and emerging defensive and offensive capability; Infosecurity Europe for the wider market and governance picture; and BSides for practitioner-led content and contact with peers. To build my OT knowledge I completed the two-day, in-person OPSWAT Academy Bootcamp, covering CNI protection, OT and industrial control system (ICS) security and threat prevention. Earlier, in policing, I completed a course in Android debugging and used specialist mobile forensic tools such as GrayKey and Cellebrite to examine locked devices. Alongside formal learning, I read industry news and articles daily to keep up with regulatory change and attacker methods.
E1.result: I passed the OPSWAT certification for the MetaDefender platform. I aim for 20 to 40 hours of formal CPD a year from training courses and conferences, and record it in my SANS account, where it counts towards recertification of my GIAC Certified Forensic Analyst (GCFA) certification, which GIAC reviews at each renewal.
E1.followup: I am attending Black Hat and BSides London in December 2026, and my GCFA recertification requirement keeps my recorded CPD on track each year.

E2.situation: Digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) and intelligence work often happens in isolated or air-gapped environments, or on client sites without approved tooling. Commercial and open-source tools are fragmented, sit behind paywalls, or run as cloud services to which sensitive data cannot be uploaded.
E2.task: I chose to contribute to the profession by building and sharing free tools, and to promote it by sharing knowledge publicly. These are personal projects: I am responsible for designing, building and maintaining the tools myself.
E2.action: I designed and built a suite of more than 40 free, open-source tools that run entirely in the browser, with development accelerated by artificial intelligence (AI). They span the incident lifecycle, from case management, email header and PowerShell analysis to file hashing, alongside MITRE ATT&CK mapping and assessment frameworks such as the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF). I also built fx, a graphical forensic triage tool that parses Windows host artefacts, hashes all evidence, and automatically hunts for the tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) and indicators of compromise (IOCs) of prolific ransomware groups. After the CrowdStrike outage in July 2024 I shared newly registered CrowdStrike domains daily on X and LinkedIn for defenders to block. I discussed AI, DFIR and cyber resilience as a guest on the Richmond Advisory Group's Cyber Sidekicks podcast in October 2025, and have contributed to coverage in the Daily Mail and on Times Radio. In policing, I gave a talk to the Bedford branch of BCS (The Chartered Institute for IT) and lectures to colleagues on the dark web, cyber crime and digital currencies.
E2.result: Both projects are public on GitHub, and fx, at version 0.1.4, has been used on real investigations by me and other users. I have shared fx with named practitioners in the industry who are testing it; their feedback has been positive about its ability to find evidence of malicious activity, and they have suggested future improvements.
E2.followup: fx is under active development, and I use that user feedback to shape it.

E3.situation: As digital forensics and incident response (DFIR) lead I saw that, without an intelligence capability, my team was limited in its ability to attribute activity, anticipate attacker behaviour and advise clients beyond the immediate incident. Clients also increasingly wanted a service covering both reactive and proactive work. I had built a similar service in my previous role, where it delivered 15% of total incident response revenue across reactive work and retainers.
E3.task: I was responsible for designing and delivering a threat intelligence offering with two aims: strengthening our incident response with timely intelligence, and establishing a standalone service with a clear market differentiator.
E3.action: I designed the workstream around the intelligence lifecycle and tested several commercial intelligence products to complement the team's own dark web persona footprint, capability and open-source tooling. As well as monitoring each client's own exposure and risk, the offering mapped their critical supply chain, assessed through stakeholder interviews, and monitored that supply chain at a high level, for example flagging that a supplier had 50 infostealer malware infections in the past month, or that a supplier holding the client's data had suffered a ransomware attack. This helped clients understand and act on supply chain risk. I took the product to market with the marketing team.
E3.result: Intelligence quickly became part of our incident response process: from the outset the team gathered current tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs), indicators of compromise (IOCs) and campaign intelligence to support engagements, speeding up detection of malicious activity. Client feedback on the launch was positive, and supply chain coverage was a major factor in its success, helped by launching at a time of several high-profile ransomware incidents enabled by supply chain compromise.
E3.followup: I keep the wider community informed through a threat intelligence webinar, open to all, which has grown without advertising to 125 attendees from more than 15 countries. Following attendee feedback it now runs quarterly with a sector focus.
